clue.text: Turner's Ferry Terminal is a replica, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests these letters are only one possible arrangement, so they are to be reordered

explanation.surface: A painting by Turner of a ferry terminal turns out to be a copy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges all ten letters of IS A REPLICA. Turner's 1803 painting shows the harbour at the French Channel port.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. W. Turner painted the crowded harbour jetty of the French port, a canvas now in the National Gallery.

clue.text: Nothing supporting injured bird in north wind

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece that supports sits underneath, so it comes last
injured suggests the bird's name is damaged, its letters knocked into a new order

parts.note: a quail is a small game bird
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A wounded bird propped up by nothing out in a northerly gale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'injured' mixes QUAIL into AQUIL; 'supporting' puts O below it in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman mythology the god of the cold northern gale was named this, the Latin counterpart of Boreas.

clue.text: Literary monthly is all at sea

definitions.meaning: a long-running Boston magazine of letters and politics, founded in 1857
an ocean, which is nothing but sea

explanation.definitionFit: The American magazine bears the ocean's name, and that ocean is entirely open water between Europe and the Americas.

clue.text: Repeated bloomers by Van Gogh

parts.note: the Dutch painter returned again and again to vases of tall yellow flowers, painting several versions

explanation.surface: Van Gogh keeps making the same blunders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomers' looks like mistakes (or underwear) but means flowers; Van Gogh painted his famous yellow-flower still life in several versions.
explanation.definitionFit: Van Gogh's celebrated series of still lifes shows yellow blooms in vases, painted repeatedly at Arles.

clue.text: Poem, I note, is very pleasant

parts.note: an idyll is a short pastoral poem
C is a musical note

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a poem is delightful.
explanation.definitionFit: Something peaceful and charming, like an idealised country scene, is described with this word.

clue.text: Artist with upcoming British pottery in Japanese style

parts.note: RA, a Royal Academician, is the crossword's standard artist

indicators.note: in a down clue upcoming means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: UK is the abbreviation for United Kingdom, standing for British

explanation.surface: A painter teams up with a rising British potter working in a Japanese manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upcoming' turns UK into KU beneath RA.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a hand-moulded, low-fired Japanese ware traditionally used for tea ceremony bowls.

clue.text: Margaret Oliphant presented his better half

definitions.text: Margaret Oliphant presented his better half

parts.words: Margaret Oliphant presented his better half
parts.note: the Victorian novelist wrote a book named after a clergyman's wife, so it is his spouse she presented

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist introduced a man's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Oliphant's 1869 novel was 'The Minister's Wife'; 'better half' is a jokey term for a spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliphant's novel title names a clergyman whose wife is its subject.

clue.text: Larger lads make vowel shift in Murillo's work

indicators.note: the vowels of the first word change, I becoming E and E becoming A

parts.note: larger means bigger
lads are boys

explanation.surface: Bigger youths produce a change of vowels in a Spanish painter's picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make vowel shift' turns BIGGER into EGGAR spellings: I to E and E to A, giving a word for a mendicant.
explanation.definitionFit: Murillo, the Spanish Baroque painter, made several genre scenes of ragged street urchins of Seville.

clue.text: Smollett's counsel in announcement might be gripping

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken, so the words are heard rather than read

parts.note: a vice is a tool that grips, so the phrase gives A VICE

explanation.surface: A lawyer's statement in a public notice could hold the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Smollett wrote a 1746 verse satire called 'Advice'; spoken, it sounds like 'a vice', the gripping tool (spelt vise in the US).
explanation.definitionFit: Counsel and guidance mean the same, and Smollett's satirical poem bears that title.

clue.text: "The wind groaned — among the lofty branches above" (Ann Radcliffe)

definitions.text: "The wind groaned — among the lofty branches above" (Ann Radcliffe)

parts.words: The wind groaned — among the lofty branches above" (Ann Radcliffe
parts.note: a quotation from the Gothic novelist with a gap for the adverb describing how the wind groaned

explanation.surface: A gloomy line of Gothic prose with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank clue: the missing adverb completes Radcliffe's sentence about a moody, morose wind.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in a gloomy, morose manner, fitting a wind that groans.

clue.text: How Wodehouse left us (with the vapours?)

definitions.text: How Wodehouse left us (with the vapours?)

parts.words: How Wodehouse left us (with the vapours?
parts.note: Wodehouse's comic novel title pairs this word with gas, a vapour, and his books leave readers merry

explanation.surface: The state P. G. Wodehouse put readers in, perhaps with a dose of fumes.
explanation.walkthrough: Wodehouse wrote 'Laughing Gas' (1936); nitrous oxide is the vapour, and his readers are left in fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Wodehouse's readers end in merriment, and his novel title adds gas, the anaesthetic vapour.

clue.text: Maurice Baring's was quite seamless

parts.note: the novelist Maurice Baring wrote a book about a garment without a seam, recalling Christ's robe

explanation.surface: Praise for how smoothly an Edwardian writer's work holds together.
explanation.walkthrough: Baring's 1929 novel is 'The Coat Without Seam'; 'seamless' looks like praise for his prose.
explanation.definitionFit: Baring's title names an outer garment woven in one piece, like the robe at the Crucifixion.

clue.text: General subject of Beethoven overture

definitions.meaning: Beethoven wrote an 1807 concert overture for Collin's play about him

explanation.definitionFit: Caius Marcius, the Roman soldier of legend, is Shakespeare's tragic hero and the topic of Beethoven's overture.

clue.text: De Quincey was an English one

definitions.text: De Quincey was an English one

parts.words: De Quincey was an English one
parts.note: Thomas De Quincey's famous Confessions describe himself as an English user of laudanum

explanation.surface: A remark about a Romantic essayist's nationality.
explanation.walkthrough: The book is 'Confessions of an English Opium-Eater' (1821).
explanation.definitionFit: De Quincey's memoir title calls him an addict of the drug laudanum.

clue.text: She refused at least one coronet, said her niece Sophia

definitions.text: She refused at least one coronet, said her niece Sophia

parts.words: She refused at least one coronet, said her niece Sophia
parts.note: in Fielding's Tom Jones, Sophia's aunt boasts of having turned down titled suitors

explanation.surface: A family story about an aunt who turned down a peerage.
explanation.walkthrough: In Fielding's 'Tom Jones' Sophia's aunt, Squire Western's sister, prides herself on having refused aristocratic offers of marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Squire Western's sister in Tom Jones is Sophia's aunt, a woman proud of rejecting noble suitors.

clue.text: Answered, like a repeat performance?

explanation.definitionFit: Responding is one sense; split as re-acted it means staged a second time, as in a repeat show.

clue.text: Dominant type with strange use for river god

parts.note: an alpha is the dominant member of a group

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters of the following word are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: A bossy character uses a river deity in an odd way.
explanation.walkthrough: Alpheus was the Greek river god who pursued the nymph Arethusa under the sea to Sicily; 'strange' is the anagram signal for 'use'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the god of the Peloponnesian river chased the nymph Arethusa.

clue.text: The subject is grass (difficult to parse)

indicators.note: difficult suggests the words are troublesome, so their letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson concedes that the topic is grass, a hard word to analyse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'difficult' rearranges TO PARSE.
explanation.definitionFit: This tough Mediterranean plant is used for cordage, paper and baskets.

clue.text: Finding a sort of bug in a remake of Lear? It may be debated

indicators.note: a sort of signals a variety of the insect's name, its letters rearranged
a remake reshapes the play's name, so its letters are mixed too

explanation.surface: Discovering an insect in a new version of King Lear is a debating point.
explanation.walkthrough: BUG, A and LEAR are all mixed together: 'a sort of' and 'remake of' both call for rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A point open to dispute is one people can contest.

clue.text: Eris sowed it with an apple

definitions.text: Eris sowed it with an apple

parts.words: Eris sowed it with an apple
parts.note: the Greek goddess of strife threw a golden apple among the goddesses, starting the quarrel behind the Trojan War

explanation.surface: A mythological goddess planted something using fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Eris tossed a golden apple marked 'for the fairest' at a wedding feast, setting Hera, Athena and Aphrodite at odds.
explanation.definitionFit: Eris was goddess of strife, and her golden apple is proverbially the apple of dissension.

clue.text: Overwhelming pop verses I rewrite

indicators.note: rewriting the words recasts them, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A songwriter reworks the lyrics of a pop song to make it powerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewrite' rearranges POP, VERSES and I together.
explanation.definitionFit: Heat or authority that crushes and weighs heavily is described with this word.

clue.text: First genuinely amusing pilot script shows certain lacunae

indicators.note: first tells us to take the opening letter of each following word

explanation.surface: A truly funny draft for a TV pilot still has holes.
explanation.walkthrough: Lacunae are missing pieces or blanks in a text.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacunae are holes or blank spaces, especially missing passages in a manuscript.

clue.text: Novelist's bird which travelled from Rouen to Barnes

definitions.text: Novelist's bird which travelled from Rouen to Barnes

parts.words: Novelist's bird which travelled from Rouen to Barnes
parts.note: Flaubert of Rouen kept a stuffed bird on his desk, and Julian Barnes made it the title of his novel

explanation.surface: A writer's pet bird flies from Normandy to a London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnes looks like the London district, but it is Julian Barnes, author of 'Flaubert's Parrot' (1984); Flaubert lived near Rouen.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaubert borrowed a stuffed one to write 'Un coeur simple', and Barnes's novel hunts for it.

clue.text: Don describes crude murals by Auden

definitions.meaning: Auden's book of clerihews is titled with this word followed by graffiti, rough wall scrawls

explanation.definitionFit: A university lecturer is one, and Auden's collection of comic verses is called 'Academic Graffiti'.

clue.text: Additional subject for Peter Ackroyd

definitions.meaning: Ackroyd wrote a biography of Sir Thomas, Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor

explanation.definitionFit: It means extra, and it is the surname of the Tudor saint whose life Ackroyd wrote in 1998.

clue.text: Poet identifies position of plane nearing Manchester

parts.note: an aircraft in flight is above things, over them
Bury is a town just north of Manchester

explanation.surface: A poet works out where an aircraft is as it approaches Manchester.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Thomas Overbury was a Jacobean poet, poisoned in the Tower of London; BURY is a town in Greater Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas Overbury wrote 'A Wife' and the Characters, and was murdered in 1613.

clue.text: Posh, more confident Shylock

parts.note: U means upper-class, as in U and non-U speech
surer means more confident

explanation.surface: A snobbish, increasingly self-assured moneylender.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the old label for upper-class usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Shylock, Shakespeare's moneylender, charges interest, and his name is used generically for any lender at extortionate rates.

clue.text: Tone poem encouraging a prime minister, they say,

indicators.note: they say indicates the phrase is heard aloud rather than spelt

parts.note: to egg on is to urge, and Edward Heath was a British prime minister

explanation.surface: A piece of music that cheers on a head of government.
explanation.walkthrough: Holst's orchestral work is named after Hardy's fictional heath; said aloud it sounds like 'egg on Heath', urging Edward Heath (UK prime minister 1970-74).
explanation.definitionFit: Holst's 1927 orchestral piece evokes the bleak Wessex moorland of Hardy's novels.
